title: Building Projects: Flags, Make, and CMake
summary: Pick the compiler flags that matter, compile files separately, let make rebuild only what changed, and describe an include, src, and tests project in CMake.
intro: Until now every program was one file and one command. A real project is dozens of files, built many times a day by you, by a server that checks each change, and once more for the release that trades. This lesson covers the compiler flags that change what you get, why C++ compiles each file on its own, how `make` rebuilds only what changed, and how CMake describes a project laid out in `include/`, `src/`, and `tests/`.

steps.title: Compiler flags that change your program
steps.body:
A backtest that takes 8 seconds on a teammate's machine takes 80 on yours. The code is the same, but the build isn't: yours was compiled without `-O2`. Flags change the program you get. clang and g++ take the same ones, and MSVC spells them its own way:

| Flag | What it does | MSVC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-std=c++17` | picks the language version | `/std:c++17` |
| `-O0`, `-O2`, `-O3` | how hard to optimize | `/Od`, `/O2` |
| `-g` | adds debug info for `lldb` and `gdb` | `/Zi` |
| `-Wall -Wextra` | warns about likely bugs | `/W4` |
| `-Werror` | turns warnings into errors | `/WX` |
| `-march=native` | uses every instruction this CPU has | `/arch:AVX2` |
| `-Iinclude`, `-DNAME` | adds a header folder, defines a macro | `/I`, `/D` |

Here is what each one did on a Mac with Apple clang 21:

- **`-std`**: *From Source to Executable: Preprocess, Compile, Link* showed that plain `clang++` here builds C++14. Then the `std::optional` from *Infinity, Sentinels, and Null* fails with `error: no template named 'optional' in namespace 'std'`. g++ 10.2 and MSVC default to C++14 too, so always pass it.
- **`-O`**: a loop that updates 2 × 10^7 integers ten times took about 0.8 s at `-O0` and 0.08 s at `-O2`, with the same output. Debug at `-O0`, ship at `-O2`. *Measuring Speed: Benchmarks, -O2, and Assembly*, in the advanced track, shows what the optimizer does.
- **`-g`**: one object file grew from 4,936 to 110,928 bytes, all of it debug info, while its machine code stayed at 1,280 bytes. It costs nothing at run time, so release builds often keep it.
- **`-march=native`**: lets the compiler use instructions your CPU has beyond the baseline, like AVX2 on x86. Apple Silicon spells it `-mcpu=native`, and on a recent Apple Silicon Mac it raised the `__ARM_FEATURE_` macros clang defines from 26 to 33, among them `__ARM_FEATURE_SME2`, a matrix unit that older Apple chips lack. Such a program may die with `Illegal instruction` on an older machine, so build for the oldest CPU you deploy to.
- **`-Wall -Wextra`**: that lesson said to read every warning, and these two ask for many more. Plain `clang++` flagged one problem in a small file, and with these it flagged three, among them a fee function that ignored its `rate` parameter:

```text
warn.cpp:5:23: warning: comparison of integers of different signs: 'int' and 'size_type' (aka 'unsigned long') [-Wsign-compare]
    5 |     for (int i = 0; i < sizes.size(); ++i) {
warn.cpp:13:36: warning: unused parameter 'rate' [-Wunused-parameter]
   13 | double fee(double notional, double rate) {
warn.cpp:23:1: warning: non-void function does not return a value in all control paths [-Wreturn-type]
```

Add `-Werror` and all three stop the build, which is how a team keeps warnings from piling up. g++ prints the same three with its own wording.

example.title: A build banner
example.prompt: Print what the optimization and CPU flags did to this build, read from the macros they define, as a server might log at startup.
example.output:
optimized: yes
inlining: on
widest SIMD: SSE2, the x86-64 baseline
example.explanation: The sandbox builds each file at `-O0` and C++17 unless its first line asks for more, and `// -O2` here asks for what `g++ -O2` does in a terminal. A first line of `// -std=c++20` turns on C++20 the same way, and *What C++20 and C++23 Add* uses it. Each flag leaves a mark the preprocessor can test: any level above `-O0` defines `__OPTIMIZE__`, and `-O0` defines `__NO_INLINE__`, because it pastes no function's body into its callers. Nothing passed `-march`, so g++ targets the x86-64 baseline. Every x86-64 CPU has SSE2, so `__SSE2__` is always on, while `__AVX2__` stays undefined whatever the CPU underneath can do. Delete the first line and run it again: `optimized: no` and `inlining: off`. A service that logs these lines at startup shows a slow release to be a debug build in seconds.

practice.title: What this build is tuned for
practice.prompt:
Report from the compiler's macros what a build of this file is tuned for. Its first line, `// -Os`, builds it for small code, the way `g++ -Os` does.

1. Print `optimization: size` when `__OPTIMIZE_SIZE__` is defined, `optimization: speed` when only `__OPTIMIZE__` is, and `optimization: none` otherwise.
2. Print `inlining: off` when `__NO_INLINE__` is defined, and `inlining: on` otherwise.
3. Print `popcount: one instruction` when `__POPCNT__` is defined, which `-mpopcnt` or a `-march` for a newer CPU turns on, and `popcount: library call` otherwise.

Expected output:

```text
optimization: size
inlining: on
popcount: library call
```

tests.output:
optimization: size
inlining: on
popcount: library call

hints: Test `__OPTIMIZE_SIZE__` first, since `-Os` defines `__OPTIMIZE__` too: `#if defined(__OPTIMIZE_SIZE__)`, then `#elif defined(__OPTIMIZE__)`.
Each of the other two lines is one `#ifdef`, an `#else`, and an `#endif`, as in the example.

steps.title: Separate compilation
steps.body:
*Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker* built three files with `-c` and one link, and noted that an edit to one `.cpp` recompiles only that file. Here is what that's worth, measured on a Mac, for a project laid out the way the rest of this lesson builds toward:

```text
quotes/
  include/
    fees.h        kFeeRate and fee()
    quote.h       mid() and spreadBps()
  src/
    fees.cpp      includes fees.h
    quote.cpp     includes quote.h
    main.cpp      includes both, plus <iostream> and <iomanip>
```

One command could build it all, `clang++ -std=c++17 -Iinclude src/*.cpp -o app`, but then every build recompiles every file. Instead, compile each `.cpp` to its object file, then link the objects. `-Iinclude` adds `include/` to the folders that `#include "quote.h"` searches, so headers and sources can live apart:

```bash
clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Iinclude -c src/fees.cpp -o build/fees.o
clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Iinclude -c src/quote.cpp -o build/quote.o
clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Iinclude -c src/main.cpp -o build/main.o
clang++ build/fees.o build/quote.o build/main.o -o app
```

This is **separate compilation**: each translation unit compiles without looking at the others, so its object file stays valid until one of its inputs changes. g++ on Linux takes the same commands, and MSVC's `cl /c` makes `.obj` files the same way.

The timings show why it pays. `fees.cpp` and `quote.cpp` compiled in about 0.01 s each, `main.cpp` in 0.23 s, and the link took 0.02 s. `main.cpp` is slow because `<iostream>` and `<iomanip>` paste in 64,737 lines, the pasting *From Source to Executable: Preprocess, Compile, Link* measured for `<iostream>`, against 29 lines for `quote.cpp`. Edit `fees.cpp` and you rerun one 0.01 s compile and the link. In a codebase of 2,000 files at a second each, that turns half an hour into seconds.

Headers are the catch. An object depends on its `.cpp` and on every header that file includes, so editing `quote.h` recompiles both `quote.cpp` and `main.cpp`. A header that every file includes, like a big `common.h`, turns each edit to it into a full rebuild. Keep headers small, and include only what a file uses.

example.title: What an edit recompiles
example.prompt: For the quotes project, list the source files each edit forces to recompile, and how many preprocessed lines that means.
example.output:
edit src/fees.cpp: src/fees.cpp (26 lines)
edit include/quote.h: src/main.cpp src/quote.cpp (64766 lines)
edit include/fees.h: src/fees.cpp src/main.cpp (64763 lines)
example.explanation: A source must recompile when it is the file you edited or when it includes that file, which is what the inner loop checks. Editing `fees.cpp` touches one small translation unit. Editing either header also recompiles `main.cpp`, and with it the 64,737 lines that `<iostream>` and `<iomanip>` paste in. That's why a one-line change to a header can cost a thousand times more compiling than the same change in a `.cpp`. A real build tool works this out from the files themselves, as the next part shows.

practice.title: A header everyone includes
practice.prompt:
List what each edit recompiles in a bigger project where every source includes common.h.

1. In `showEdit`, print `edit `, the edited file, and `:`.
2. Print a space and the name of each source that is the edited file or includes it, in the order of `kSources`.
3. End the line with ` (k of n files)`, where `k` is how many sources you printed and `n` is how many there are.

Expected output:

```text
edit src/risk.cpp: src/risk.cpp (1 of 4 files)
edit include/book.h: src/book.cpp src/main.cpp (2 of 4 files)
edit include/common.h: src/book.cpp src/feed.cpp src/main.cpp src/risk.cpp (4 of 4 files)
```

tests.output:
edit src/risk.cpp: src/risk.cpp (1 of 4 files)
edit include/book.h: src/book.cpp src/main.cpp (2 of 4 files)
edit include/common.h: src/book.cpp src/feed.cpp src/main.cpp src/risk.cpp (4 of 4 files)

hints: Follow the example's `showEdit`, counting files instead of adding up lines.
`kSources.size()` gives the `n` at the end of each line.

steps.title: A Makefile rebuilds what changed
steps.body:
Remembering which of those commands to rerun is a build tool's job. `make` reads a **Makefile** of rules. A rule names a **target**, the files it's made from (its **prerequisites**), and the commands that make it, each indented with a tab. `make` rebuilds a target when it is missing or older than any prerequisite, after bringing each prerequisite up to date the same way. File modification times are the whole mechanism. Here is the quotes project's Makefile:

```text
CXX      := clang++
CXXFLAGS := -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror
CPPFLAGS := -Iinclude -MMD -MP

SRCS := $(wildcard src/*.cpp)
OBJS := $(patsubst src/%.cpp,build/%.o,$(SRCS))

app: $(OBJS)
	$(CXX) $(OBJS) -o $@

build/%.o: src/%.cpp
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CPPFLAGS) $(CXXFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

clean:
	rm -rf build app

-include $(OBJS:.o=.d)

.PHONY: clean
```

`:=` sets a variable and `$(CXX)` reads it. `build/%.o: src/%.cpp` is a **pattern rule**, where `%` matches any name, `$<` is the first prerequisite, and `$@` is the target. GNU Make 3.81 on a Mac, from a clean folder, again with nothing changed, and after two edits (`touch` only updates a file's time):

```text
$ make
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/fees.cpp -o build/fees.o
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/main.cpp -o build/main.o
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/quote.cpp -o build/quote.o
clang++ build/fees.o build/main.o build/quote.o -o app
$ make
make: `app' is up to date.
$ touch src/fees.cpp && make
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/fees.cpp -o build/fees.o
clang++ build/fees.o build/main.o build/quote.o -o app
$ touch include/quote.h && make
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/main.cpp -o build/main.o
clang++ -Iinclude -MMD -MP -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c src/quote.cpp -o build/quote.o
clang++ build/fees.o build/main.o build/quote.o -o app
```

Make knows that `main.o` needs `quote.h` only because of `-MMD`, which makes the compiler write a file like `build/main.d` next to each object, listing the project headers it really read (system headers such as `<iostream>` are left out). `-include` reads those lists back in:

```text
build/main.o: src/main.cpp include/fees.h include/quote.h
include/fees.h:
include/quote.h:
```

The first version of this Makefile had neither. After lowering `kFeeRate` in `fees.h` from 5 to 3 basis points, `make` said `app` was up to date, and the program still charged 15.1890 instead of 9.1134. A stale build like that is worse than a failed one. `-MP` adds the empty `include/fees.h:` rules, so a renamed header doesn't stop make with a `No rule to make target` error.

Indent a command with spaces and make stops with `Makefile:9: *** missing separator.  Stop.`. `make -j8` runs up to 8 commands at once, and `make clean` deletes the outputs. `.PHONY` says that `clean` is a command, not a file. Linux has the same GNU make, while Windows projects mostly use CMake, next.

example.title: Make's rebuild rule
example.prompt: Walk the quotes project's rules the way make does after quote.h is saved, and print what it rebuilds and why.
example.output:
build/fees.o is up to date
rebuild build/main.o (include/quote.h is newer)
rebuild build/quote.o (include/quote.h is newer)
rebuild app (build/main.o is newer)
example.explanation: Each rule is a list with the target first, like a Makefile line `target: prerequisites`. A target is rebuilt when any prerequisite's time is later than its own. `fees.o`, at 100, is newer than everything it needs, so it stays. `quote.h`, saved at 200, is newer than `main.o` and `quote.o`, so both are rebuilt and get the current time. That makes them newer than `app`, which was linked at 103, so `app` is relinked too. The objects' rules come before `app`'s, so a rebuilt object is always ready before the program that links it. Real make finds that order itself by following the prerequisites.

practice.title: A missing object
practice.prompt:
Walk the same rules after fees.cpp is saved and build/main.o is deleted.

1. A time of 0 means the file doesn't exist. A missing target is rebuilt with the reason `missing`: print `rebuild ` and the target, then ` (missing)`.
2. Otherwise, rebuild a target whose first newer prerequisite is found, printing it as the example does, or print the target followed by ` is up to date`.
3. Give each rebuilt target the time `now`, then add 1 to `now`.

Expected output:

```text
rebuild build/fees.o (src/fees.cpp is newer)
rebuild build/main.o (missing)
build/quote.o is up to date
rebuild app (build/fees.o is newer)
```

tests.output:
rebuild build/fees.o (src/fees.cpp is newer)
rebuild build/main.o (missing)
build/quote.o is up to date
rebuild app (build/fees.o is newer)

hints: Start from the example's loop, and check for a time of 0 before looking for a newer prerequisite.
`app` names `build/fees.o` as the reason, because it is the first prerequisite in its rule that is newer.

steps.title: CMake and the include, src, tests layout
steps.body:
A Makefile is tied to one toolchain: `clang++`, `-MMD`, and `rm -rf` mean nothing to MSVC. **CMake** is a build system generator. You describe the project once in `CMakeLists.txt`, and CMake writes a Makefile, a Ninja file, or a Visual Studio solution for whichever machine runs it, with dependency tracking built in. Most C++ projects you'll clone use it. CMake doesn't come with macOS or Apple's command line tools, so this part shows the files and commands and describes what they print. Install it with `brew install cmake`, or your Linux package manager, to run them. This is the layout to aim for, with the tests beside the code:

```text
quotes/
  CMakeLists.txt
  include/   fees.h  quote.h          the library's interface
  src/       fees.cpp  quote.cpp      the library
             main.cpp                 the program
  tests/     test_quote.cpp           a program that checks the library
```

```text
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(quotes LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

if(MSVC)
  add_compile_options(/W4 /WX)
else()
  add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Werror)
endif()

add_library(quotes_core src/fees.cpp src/quote.cpp)
target_include_directories(quotes_core PUBLIC include)

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE quotes_core)

enable_testing()
add_executable(test_quote tests/test_quote.cpp)
target_link_libraries(test_quote PRIVATE quotes_core)
add_test(NAME test_quote COMMAND test_quote)
```

A **target** is something to build. `quotes_core` is a static library of the shared code, and both `app` and `test_quote` link it, so that code compiles once. `PUBLIC include` means the folder is part of the library's interface, so whatever links `quotes_core` gets `-Iinclude` too, where `PRIVATE` would keep it to the library's own files. The three `CMAKE_CXX_` lines make CMake pass `-std=c++17`. Build out of source, in a `build/` folder you can delete at any time:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j 8
./build/app
ctest --test-dir build
```

The first command **configures**: it finds your compiler, prints a few lines starting with `--`, and writes the build files into `build/`. The second runs them, printing a percentage and a line for each object it compiles and each target it links. `ctest` runs every program named in an `add_test` and counts it passed when it exits with status 0.

`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` picks the flags: `Debug` adds `-g`, `Release` adds `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, and `RelWithDebInfo` adds `-O2 -g -DNDEBUG`, where `-DNDEBUG` removes every `assert`, as *The Preprocessor: Macros and Conditional Compilation* showed. Leave it out and you get no optimization at all, the slow build from the first part. Visual Studio picks the type when building instead, with `cmake --build build --config Release`.

Real projects add a few tools around this. A package manager, vcpkg or Conan, fetches libraries such as GoogleTest and hands them to CMake. `clang-format` keeps every file in one style, `clang-tidy` flags bug patterns the compiler lets through, and `ccache` reuses object files a clean build would otherwise redo. Two more flags trade build time for speed: `-flto`, link-time optimization, lets the optimizer inline across translation units, and profile-guided optimization (`-fprofile-generate`, a typical run, then `-fprofile-use`) rebuilds the program with what that run measured.

example.title: A test program for the library
example.prompt: Check the quotes library from a test program, the kind ctest runs, in one file standing in for include, src, and tests.
example.output:
pass: mid of 100 and 102 is 101
pass: a locked quote has no spread
pass: 99 and 101 are 200 bps apart
0 failed
example.explanation: A test is an ordinary program that links the library, calls it with known inputs, and compares the results. `ctest` doesn't read the printed lines. It only looks at the exit status, which is why `main` returns 1 when a check fails. The first two checks compare with `==`, which is fine because 101.0 and 0.0 come out exact. The spread of 99 and 101 is 2 over 100 times 10,000, and 0.02 has no exact binary form, so the third check accepts anything within 10^-9 of 200. The next lesson, *Testing C++: assert, a Tiny Test Harness, and Frameworks*, turns `check` into a reusable harness.

practice.title: Testing a minimum fee
practice.prompt:
Run the fee tests, fix the bug they catch in the library, and make the test program report failure the way ctest expects.

1. Run the starter: one check fails, because `mkt::fee` never applies the broker's minimum.
2. Fix `fee` so it returns `kMinFee` whenever `notional * kFeeRate` is below it.
3. Make `main` return 1 when any check failed and 0 when none did.

Expected output:

```text
pass: 10000 notional pays 5.00
pass: 200 notional pays the 1.00 minimum
pass: 2000 notional pays 1.00
0 failed
```

tests.output:
pass: 10000 notional pays 5.00
pass: 200 notional pays the 1.00 minimum
pass: 2000 notional pays 1.00
0 failed

hints: A ternary picks the larger of the two: `byRate < kMinFee ? kMinFee : byRate`.
End `main` as the example does: `return failures == 0 ? 0 : 1;`.

recap:
- Always pass `-std=c++17`, since Apple clang, g++ 10.2, and MSVC all default to C++14.
- `-O2` made a loop ten times faster than `-O0`. `-g` adds debug info without changing the machine code.
- `-Wall -Wextra` catch signed comparisons, unused parameters, and missing returns, and `-Werror` keeps them out (`/W4 /WX` on MSVC).
- `-march=native`, or `-mcpu=native` on Apple Silicon, uses your CPU's newest instructions, so the program may not run on an older one.
- Separate compilation turns each `.cpp` into an object with `-c`, so an edit recompiles only the files whose inputs changed, then relinks.
- A header edit recompiles every file that includes it. Keep headers small.
- `make` rebuilds a target that is missing or older than a prerequisite. Without `-MMD -MP` and `-include`, a header edit rebuilds nothing.
- CMake describes targets in `CMakeLists.txt`: a library from `src/`, a program, and tests from `tests/`, with `include/` as the library's public folder.
- Configure with `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`, build with `cmake --build build`, and run `ctest`, which passes a test that exits with 0.

Next, **Testing C++: assert, a Tiny Test Harness, and Frameworks** grows the `check` function into a test harness, then meets GoogleTest and Catch2.
